newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Pharmacia & Upjohn shares plunge after profit warning.
newsitem.headline: Pharmacia & Upjohn shares plunge after profit warning.

text.p: Pharmacia & Upjohn, the giant U.S.-Swedish pharmaceutical group, issued a surprise profit warning Wednesday, sending the company's share price plummeting.
P&U released a statement saying its sales fell by 6 percent in the first three months of the year and it expected its earnings per share before non-recurring items to drop by about 16 percent.
The group's shares plunged on the news, diving 39 crowns to 234 crowns on the Stockholm Stock Exchange and by $4.125 to $30.75 on the New York Stock Exchange.
"It was a profit warning and it was unexpected," UBS analyst Birgit Kullhoff said in an initial reaction to the news. "A profit warning is always bad news."
Most analysts were withholding comment until after hearing what the company had to say at an analysts' telephone conference call later in the day.
The markets have been unpleasantly surprised several times in the past by P&U, which was formed in November 1995 by a merger between Michigan-based Upjohn and Sweden's Pharmacia.
An analyst from a London-based securities house said P&U's problem was that its product portfolio was too mature and it needed to throw its weight behind new products.
"The problem is that there are not too many new products," he said.
P&U attributed its first-quarter sales shortfall to adverse exchange rate movements and customer inventory adjustments after a strong final quarter in 1996.
Weaker demand in Europe, particularly Germany and Sweden, and generic competition in the United States also ate into sales, the company said.
Chief Financial Officer Bob Salisbury told journalists on a telephone conference call that some of the negative factors seen hitting the first quarter were not expected to continue.
"Some of the factors will moderate and not have as adverse an effect on results in following quarters," Salisbury said.
However, he refused to give forecasts for the rest of the year.
"We don't give detailed forecasts," he said. "There is still a fair amount of uncertainty."
